topic: how applications are read (file flow / routing)
speaker_role: former admissions director (Swarthmore) and former assistant director (Vanderbilt), per his own statement
commercial_incentive: Sells a paid application-review service and pitches it in the video.
key_insights: Highly selective offices route each file through a preset path so tens of thousands of applications can be decided in a few months; readers do not give every file equal time.
An academic rating (built from rigor, GPA, rank or estimated rank, and tests if submitted) is the anchor that decides who reads a file and how deeply.
Low-rated files may get only an abbreviated review, essentially a data check and sign-off toward denial; the cutoff differs by college, major and applicant type.
Files with institutional priorities such as recruited athletes or legacies can go to a special committee regardless of the first reader's recommendation.
Some offices use part-time seasonal outside readers for a first pass on mid-range files, with an admissions officer deciding next steps only if the outside reader recommends admit.
In an output-based routing example, files get a final 0-4 rating; 1 means recommend deny, and he says roughly half to 70 percent of regular-decision files land there.
Files with missing or questionable pieces go to an 'undetermined' or additional-review bin, and suspected fraud (rare, often international) triggers an investigation.
Applicants cannot see their rating or the routing system, so the practical advice is to control application quality and build a balanced list.
specific_numbers_or_facts: Hoffman: as a new officer he was responsible for about 1,500 applications in his territory and read all of them at Swarthmore.
Hoffman (fictitious example): academic rating 4- out of 5 for a 1450 SAT, top 15 percent, very demanding curriculum.
Hoffman: 50 to 70 percent of regular-decision files receive a final rating of 1 (recommend deny).

Hoffman (fictitious example): at an 8 percent admit rate, a 31 ACT with top 10 percent gets a 3- and an abbreviated review; abbreviated-review threshold varies (3 arts and sciences, 3+ engineering, 3- journalism, 4+ international need-based aid).
Hoffman: less selective colleges may publish GPA/test formulas, e.g. illustrative 1200 SAT and 3.0 GPA auto-admit, with borderline files getting a short committee review.
notable_or_distinctive: Explains the concept of file flow and shows illustrative routing charts by academic rating, which is rarely covered elsewhere.
reliability_notes: Charts are explicitly fictitious composites, and he says practices vary by college; the video opens with a sales pitch for his review service.
